title: MTG Marvel's new Darkhold card is like an evil One Ring
content:
Wizards of the Coast revealed its next MTG Marvel product at New York Comic Con, and the new superhero set has some suitably dastardly cards. Case in point: The Darkhold. This legendary artifact is like The One Ring, only edgier.

More specifically, it's a three-mana black card you can tap to add a 'sin counter'. You then draw a card for each sin counter on The Darkhold, and you lose one life for each card in your hand.

Card draw alone feels great, even at such a deadly price. Things get better if you can spend 6BB, though. Tap The Darkhold, and each player's life total becomes equal to the lowest life total among all players. This can only be done as a Sorcery, but still. If you've been hurting yourself dabbling with the Darkhold a lot you could drag your opponents down to your own level, then swing for the kill.

The Darkhold feels riskier than The One Ring, but the rewards might be more explosive. Still, for lovers of consistency, The One Ring's slow, steady influx of cards remains more appealing. It also offers ETB protection that makes it hard to rival, not to mention a colorless casting cost. The Darkhold probably isn't quite the meta-breaker its Middle-earth counter part is, but it's still pretty fun for fans of mono-black - especially in EDH.

The Darkhold shares its name with this all-new Marvel set, Darkhold Destiny. It focuses more on the supernatural side of the Marvel universe than its predecessor. It's also the first time Wizards is using a Universes Beyond product to tell an original story.

Darkhold Destiny releases on April 9, 2027. If you want more MTG news before then, you can check out our full MTG release schedule and MTG sets guides - or catch up with our daily news stories in the Wargamer Discord.

title: New MTG Marvel set stars a brand-new character in an original dimension-hopping story
content:
At New York Comic Con today, Wizards of the Coast announced its next MTG Marvel set, MTG Marvel: Darkhold Destiny, which will feature all the supernatural and arcane elements conspicuously missing from the previous release. What is particularly exciting and interesting about this set, though, is that for the first time ever Wizards is telling an original story through a Universes Beyond product. The set, by the way, comes out pretty early next year: April 9, 2027.

It seems Darkhold Destiny isn't just a collection of magical or spooky Marvel superheroes. Wizards actually sat down with Marvel to create what the MTG Daily announcement article calls a "dimension-hopping narrative". It explores the "the secrets of the Dark Dimension", "Marvel's pantheon of gods", and explores the origins of a brand-new character that hasn't actually been introduced yet.

That character will first appear in a new Marvel comic by duo Jackson Lanzing and Collin Kelly, in February 2027, but the Magic: The Gathering set isn't just a tie-in to a coming new narrative; the "story was crafted by [Wizard's] Narrative team with Magic in mind".

This set will presumably center around the Darkhold, which if you don't know, is essentially the Marvel Comics equivalent of the Necronomicon: a mystical text of black magic. We can expect to see sorcerer characters associated with the book, like Scarlet Witch, Doctor Strange, and Morgan le Fay. Oh, and Blade will also definitely be in here, the announcement pretty explicitly teases "vampire-hunting vampires".

In fact, it might be a good idea to stop and just list all the characters teased in the Daily MTG article. I spotted:

  • Werewolf by Night
  • Blade
  • Mephisto
  • Varnae and/or Dracula

We've also already seen art or card spoilers pointing to:

  • Doctor Strange
  • Magik/Darkchild
  • Sif
  • Moon Knight
  • Hela
  • Gargantos
  • Dormammu
  • The Time Stone

Finally am I reading too much into this, or is this "Some of the most hotly anticipated Super Heroes and Super Villains will make their debut in Magic, bringing all their grim power to your decks" meant to hint at a Ghost Rider card? He's hotly and he's grim. No? Too tin-foil hat for you?

Some clever-clogs Magic fans had already looked at the character roster in MTG Marvel: Superheroes, thought about who was missing or under-represented and then determined it was likely we'd get a release showing off the magical side of the setting. But I don't think anyone anticipated Wizards contributing to another IP's story through a new Magic set.

This feels like a gigantic sea change for Universes Beyond, and I sincerely hope it's not a one-off. While it might only have been achievable because Wizards struck a long-term, multi-year partnership with Marvel, I would be so much more excited by UB sets overall if they had some actual plot to them. 'Here's that thing you know but as a Magic card' is wearing a little thin.

What do you think of this new approach to a Universes Beyond set? If you're a particularly lovely tabletop fan, we'd like to invite you to join the discussion over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: New MTG Marvel set has Arcane spells, Vengeance and Dimension mechanics
content:
We're getting a new MTG Marvel set, and with it come a slew of set-specific mechanics. Wizards of the Coast showed off several new cards at New York Comic Con today, and a few keywords in particular stand out to us: the mysterious 'Dimension', the all-new 'Vengeance', and the returning 'Arcane'.

Darkhold Destiny, releasing on April 9, 2027, is a Universes Beyond set dedicated to the supernatural side of the Marvel multiverse. Things are little darker, a little spookier, and a little more original - we're even getting all-new canon characters and storylines.

As for those keywords, let's start with the one we know most about. Arcane is an obscure subtype of Instant/Sorcery that first appeared in the Kamigawa block, in the form of 'splice onto Arcane'. This collection of words allowed you to reveal a card, pay its alternate splice cost, and then add its effects to an Arcane card.

'Splice onto Arcane' was heavily criticized at the time for being extremely parasitic, and Mark Rosewater said a few years back that it was a 9 on the Storm scale - extremely unlikely to return.

But, the head designer also said that "Arcane as a subtype on instants and sorceries that interacts in a new way" was only a 7 on the scale. So we're assuming WotC has found a new way to use them. The NYCC reveals include two Arcane cards: Hela's Arcanum and Rise from the Nether.

Next, we have Vengeance. This appears to share DNA and design space with popular existing keywords like Flashback and Adventure. Basically, it's an instant/sorcery that's bolted onto a creature card, but it's one that can only be cast from the graveyard. Once you cast it in this way, you exile it.

Hela, Mistress of Darkness has been given the Vengeance treatment. As a creature, she creates a tapped 2/2 Zombie token for every life a player loses during your turn. Her Vengeance power, however, is Dark Tutor. This searches your library for a card, putting it in your hand or graveyard. You then lose three life.

Lastly comes Dimension. I'll be honest, I have no idea what the hell Dimension is. We see the word appear on Temple of Khonshu, a land that enters tapped unless you control a Dimension. Presumably, it's a new card subtype rather than some altogether new card type, but stranger things have happened.

title: BattleTechnical: Mook Mechs
content:
A few weeks back I wrote about how to build interesting forces as a GM (game master, not General Motors, for those of you that were confused). A key part of that is picking units that give the players an interesting game and present a challenge without being too likely to knock players out early. At the same time, both sides of the table are going to get bored if you throw nothing but 5 damage hits at people – it cuts down on threat analysis and decision making, ending up with every game feeling similar. To avoid this, I tend to categorize mook mechs into a couple different groups, and make sure to include some of each in my forces.

The categories I tend to put mechs in are:

  • Brawlers
  • Flashbulbs
  • Annoyances
  • Objective-grabbers

Not all of these are going to feature in every force, and some mechs will split across multiple categories, but by mixing these I can generally create forces that are engaging to play against without ever being a true problem for players. In each of these categories I’m going to include a couple ilClan-era mechs and why I’d field them.

Dawn Guard Crusader. Credit: Jack Hunter

The Brawler

These mechs are ones that are lower on damage and higher on durability. Generally they aren’t all the way up on durability like I might take in a competitive list, and I want to avoid standard engines here unless I can use risk of ammo explosion to help speed up death. It’s where heavies and assaults (and some thicker mediums) end up. When I want to represent a siege force (attacking or defending) I usually end up sticking a few more of these in, while I’ll include fewer if I’m making a recon or striker force.

Crusader CRD-5M

Crusaders are well known for ammo bombs, and this one is no exception. With an XL engine and ammo in both side torsos (and the right arm) there are a multitude of ways for it to die, but it’s got enough armor that it won’t happen instantly. Damage is decent out of the pair of LRM 15s, but kept to 5 point groupings, and there’s good counterplay against it by getting inside minimum range.

Wolverine WVR-9R

This wolverine is a pretty decent mech without any crippling flaws, but it also isn’t doing anything tremendously well. It does moderate damage at moderate range with moderate mobility, so it can be planned around by both you and the players. One side torso is empty other than the engine, and the other is stacked full of ammo, so it’s not too hard to take out. It also rewards good play by the players – with its main gun in the right arm, it offers canny players where they can engage it without getting shot back.

Amarok

A mech that I’d never otherwise recommend using, this makes a great campaign filler. At 100 tons, moving up to 7 hexes, it’s threatening at a glance. It’s covered in hardened armor, which again makes it threatening at a glance. It’s got an OK weapon load, but doesn’t have the heat to effectively use it – and a PPC capacitor is mostly wasted potential. With only 56% coverage by the hardened armor, it gets the drawbacks (move speed reduction and PSR penalty) without actually gaining much of a durability benefit other than specifically to headshots. It’s not going to take any longer than an Atlas to die, and again rewards players who are smart enough to go for kicks and position to avoid being attacked by torso mounted weapons.

Cougar. Credit: porble

The Flashbulb

Almost the opposite of brawlers, these are mechs that do a lot of damage for their durability and often come with heat problems. Having mechs with heat problems is great, because it gives you options depending on how well players are doing – you can always throw out a bunch of fire on not-great shots, then slow down from the overheat and give the players an opportunity to remove a mech from the board. You can find them in every era and techbase, but they’re extremely common among clan mechs.

Cougar I

Most cougars are going to fall into this category, but this one does it particularly well. Improved heavy lasers are a real threat, but one without a lot of range, and firing both spikes this slow light mech up to at least 10 heat. A cougar that only has six MP should be a dead cougar.

Shadow Cat J

The flash here is mostly what’s likely to happen to the pilot. It’s got decent total damage, so it can’t be totally ignored, but every single weapon is explosive and it doesn’t have a whole lot of armor. It’s quite liable to take a couple hits and then have the pilot pass out, which can be good or bad – good if you want to let the players salvage a shadow cat, less good if you don’t.

Warhammer WHM-11T

While looking like a warhammer at a glance, this one picks up a bad move profile, enough weapons to overheat pretty badly on an alpha strike or let you do consistent moderate damage (in 10 point hits, but having some of those in a force is good as long as you don’t go super heavy on them – you want players to feel some concern), and a glaring weakness in under-armored legs. I’ve mentioned having specific weaknesses in a couple of these mechs, and I think it’s a very valuable thing to have on your OpFor mechs as it gives the players something to reward paying attention and thinking about their play.

Panther. Credit: Rockfish

The Annoyance

Annoyances are units that exist to do a bit of damage, just enough to be noticed, but are a little too durable or a little too long ranged to be a target where the players want to focus all their fire. I don’t put them in every force, because they absolutely do get annoying and can tilt the game if the players don’t have a way to deal with them, but they’re a perfect unit if players are bringing a mix of forces and have some fast units. Position them away from your main force and the players have something for their fast mechs to do without the risk of diving right into some higher damage heavies.

Panther PNT-12K

This applies equally to just about every panther; they’re all perfect annoyance units. They have one shot for 10 damage, enough to notice but not enough generally to prioritize if there are other things to shoot, and will hang out at range. Make sure that it doesn’t engage until some of the brawlers are in the fight and keep it isolated, it’ll provide a good target for any fast player units to safely participate.

LRM Carrier

While I’ve mostly talked about mechs here, LRM carriers are something that are always worth considering. They’ve got high potential damage, so players won’t want to just let them shoot, but if you set them up for indirect fire they’re usually very inaccurate, making their actual damage output relatively low. With thin armor and little movement they’re again something great for fast player units to engage while staying out of a main brawl.

Sentinel STN-6S

The sentinel (in most of its forms) is a mech with moderate speed, moderate armor, and moderate damage. This has decent range, but is putting out hardly any damage, making it another good way to fill out a force. It doesn’t have any accuracy buffs (and even has a couple weapons with substantial minimum range), making it a perfect target for faster units to go engage, If it’s left alone it’ll eventually wear down player units, so they don’t want to ignore it completely.

Simonson's Cutthroats Locust. Credit: Jack Hunter

Objective Grabbers

These are the mechs I’m least likely to field in most forces – ones that really exist just to do objectives. Usually cheap, fast, and lightly armed, they can be described as fast annoyances. I usually don’t field many of them because I want the players to be the force with specific objectives rather than being on the defensive side. Still, sometimes they can be helpful to fill in a force, even if just to give the impression of numbers without adding anything effective (be careful that doing this doesn’t cause problems with initiative sinking though).

Locust LCT-7V2

By being faster than anything my players are likely fielding I can use this to get them to think a turn or two in advance and plan where it’s likely to go. The weapon mix on it is a mess, so if players fail to plan effectively it’s not going to just tear them apart (don’t use a Locust IIC).

Stinger STG-6R

8/12/8 is the farthest jumping profile I want to field in most games, and this does it with minimal armor and minimal damage. I do want to have this speed on something designed for objectives because there does need to be a challenge to the players – a 6/9/6 objective grabber is going to die too easily to present a mission that has any real challenge, but 8/12/8 will require them to do a little more planning around where it’s likely to go and how to kill it, while still being something they can deal with even without having a force designed around killing fast stuff.

Final Thoughts

I use mechs from these categories to fill out most of my OpFors, but not all the units in them. Depending on the number of players, I’ll almost always have a few mechs that fall outside these guidelines, either because they have one or two bigger guns, more cohesive weapon loads, or are just harder to kill. Those pull double duty – they keep the force from being something that’s too easy to deal with, and they give the players salvage choices that they’re actually going to want to use.

title: Best Pokémon chase cards in 2026
content:
What are the best Pokémon chase cards in 2026? Which cards generated the most hype, which have held their value, and what should you have your fingers crossed for when you crack packs? We've done the research: these are the biggest Pokemon TCG chase cards this year.

Here's the rules. I've chosen a sample of cards for each English Pokémon set released this year. Most cards are objectively the biggest chase cards in the set, the ones that would cost you the most to buy on the secondary market. Others are personal picks, cards that I want in my binder because I think they're completely gorgeous!

Some cards are so rare I've included them in their own section. You've got pretty good odds of pulling one SIR from 80 booster packs, so which SIR you pull is an interesting question. When a card shows up in less than one in 1,000 booster packs, it's not really part of that conversation!

We have a separate guide to the most expensive Pokémon cards of all time - at the time of writing, nothing on this list is close. But give it a few years…

2026's uber-chase cards

1/6

Mega Hyper Rare cards are a feature of all the Mega Evolution sets, gold shiny cards that show up in less than one in 1,000 booster packs. If you pull a Mega Hyper Rare card, it's definitely worth a bunch of money. But it's not necessarily the most valuable card in the set, or even the most valuable version of that specific Pokémon - for example, in Ascended Heroes, the SIR version of Dragonite ex is worth more than the Mega Hyper Rare variant.

Why is that? My best theory is that Pokémon collectors value looks at least as much as they value rarity. The Mega Hyper Rares are frankly kind of gross - they look like the golden counterfeit cards you can buy all over the internet.

An altogether different matter are the RGB Mews from Pokémon 30th Celebration. These three cards look like printing errors, as if the printing press ran out of ink for one color when it made them. Their pull rate is estimated at one in a few thousand, and their value is very high - ungraded cards are selling for around $4,000.

Ascended Heroes

1/5

Ascended Heroes was the first and the biggest set of the year, and it was absolutely jam packed with cards that trainers are still clamoring for. At the time of writing, five SIRs were selling for more than $200: Team Rocket's Mewtwo ex #281, Mega Dragonite ex #290, Pikachu ex #276 AND #277, and Mega Gengar ex #284.

The prices for these make my eyes tingle: at the time of writing, ungraded copies of Mega Gengar ex and Pikachu ex #276 are both trading for near enough $1,000, and Mega Dragonite ex is $450. They are all incredibly charismatic cards, though, and despite the large pool of SIRs, I can see why they're favorites.

Check out this article by (much missed) ex-writer Callum Self, about his luck pulling Ascended Heroes!

Perfect Order

1/2

Perfect Order is a small set with a small pool of SIRs. I'm a bit of a sucker for Mega Zygarde ex #120 because I have, truthfully, no idea what's happening in its art - I just know it's incredibly loud and energetic. I'm also a big Meowth stan, so I'm happy to see that Meowth ex #121 - an energetic Meowth, rather than a sleepy or surly one - is the most valuable chase in the set. But the fact that an ungraded card is only $88 is a good sign for how much less hype there was for this set overall!

We have a separate guide with more information about Perfect Order chase cards!

Chaos Rising

1/3

Chaos Rising proved to be another fairly unpopular set, without too much fuss about its rares - except for Mega Greninja ex #116, which at $145 dollars costs $100 more than the next nearest chase card. My favorites are actually the two trainer SIRs, the chill AZ's Tranquility and punk Roxie's Performance. They're not really a paired set of cards, but they are

We have a separate guide with more information about Chaos Rising chase cards!

Pitch Black

1/2

With Pitch Black I am once again in total agreement with the market about what the coolest card in the set is - Mega Darkrai ex is incredible. This beast looks like a scrawl out of a Junji Ito manga, perfect for the nightmare Pokémon. If I had to pick a buddy for it it would be Morpeko ex, because I have never seen a better representation of the natural aggression of a hamster.

We have a separate guide with more information about Pitch Black chase cards!

30th Celebration

1/3

30th Celebration has particularly weird booster packs with. As well as the so-rare-you-should-forget-it-exists RGB Mews, there are 'Futuristic' Mew and Mewtwo, Classic Collection reprints of retro cards, and the dedicated Pikachu slot.

As a result, the most expensive cards in the set aren't regular SIRs. The reprint of Lugia from Pokémon Aquapolis is going for $240 - hype for the reprint briefly pushes the original card's market value through the roof! Then there's the reprint of Base Set Charizard, which is going for $160. Makes me feel like I'm a lad again.

It's hard to look at this set and not fantasize about opening multiple cards from the Classic Collection. If I had to narrow it down to just one, it'd be the reprint of the Illustration Rare Magikarp from 2023's Paldea Evolved, because the juxtaposition of Shinji Kanda's elegant art and the gormless fail-fish speaks to me.

We have separate guides with more information about 30th Celebration chase cards and the Classic Collection!

title: How to Paint Everything: Char's Zaku in Gundam Assemble (Updated October 9, 2026)
content:
In our How to Paint Everything Series we cover how to paint well, everything, with a look at different methods and techniques from different painters and with an eye for different skill levels. In this article, we’re covering how to paint a Zaku II from Mobile Suit Gundam, in Char Aznable's custom colors.

Changelog

  • Update (Latest): 2026-10-09 Updated to include Rockfish's process.
  • Published: 2025-08-14

Greg

The pilot known as Char Aznable is one of anime's greatest and most versatile dickheads. Also known as Casval Deikun or Quattro Bajeena (I know), he spends about 15 years betraying people and switching sides, and pilots probably a dozen different mechs. As an ace Zeon pilot and later a freelancer, he has the right (often exercised) to paint his units in the signature red color scheme that gave him his nickname, The Red Comet. We're using the first and arguably most famous of his appearances, because it's the one that has a model: the Zaku II Commander type.

The actual colors in the anime are more of a salmon pink on the limbs and a sort of medium brown-red on the body, but I prefer the colors from Gundam The Origin, which replaces those colors with more of a true red and a crimson, respectively. It doesn't hurt that I don't have good pinks in my collection, either.

First, prime black. Then, block in your base colors. For figuring out what to put where, I referred to the best source I had, the Real Grade Char's Zaku sitting on a shelf over my painting desk. If you don't have that, Google some images of robots or just wing it.

Char's Zaku, basecoated

This took a few coats. The Vallejo Game Color Bloody Red I have - this might be common to all of them or just be a problem with my particular bottle - has god-awful coverage. It took four coats over black primer to get it smooth. The Vallejo Game Color Scarlet Red did better, which is great because the bad paint covers something like 70% of the model and the good paint only goes in a few spots. I put a generous amount of Vallejo Game Color Cold Grey on the black parts, and a single dot of Vallejo Game Color Squid Pink in both the monoeye and the scope on the gun. That was pretty much it for color separation. In all cases, try not to get too much paint in the recesses, but we'll handle that in the next step anyway, so don't sweat it if you do.

Next, we apply an all-over black wash (I actually used Warhammer Black Templar Contrast paint for this) to the black parts, and a targeted pin wash of Warhammer Agrax Earthshade to the reds. This is where you can cover any parts where the red seeped into the panel lines, but do try to be careful when applying the wash. Again, you don't have to worry too much, because we're gonna fix it, but it'll make the next step easier.

Char's Zaku, basecoated and washed

Then a bit of cleanup, layering on the base colors over the washes, to clean that up. I wanted the black to stay black, so I didn't change those areas, but bringing the reds back up does a lot to make the colors pop, since they look a little muddy after just base coat and Agrax. Leave some of the darker color in the corners or recesses, but this is a good opportunity to build contrast and visual interest. Gundams are from a cartoon, and there's nothing wrong with painting them to look overly bright and saturated. These models would probably look great in a cel-shaded paint job, but I don't have the chops to do it.

Char's Zaku, basecoated and washed and cleaned up a bit

You could probably stop here and have a perfectly tabletop-ready model, but a few more steps will be quick and worth it, if you feel comfortable with a bit of highlighting. The shape of these models makes them take highlights well - they just aren't as detailed with greebles as a Warhammer model would be. Owing to the subject matter, these are largely made of big chunky shapes built to take thinned layers as volumetric highlights, and have edges that are crying out for the side of a brush.

Char's Zaku, basecoated and washed and cleaned up a bit and highlighted

So, highlight the Scarlet Red with Bloody Red, and the Bloody Red with Hot Orange (this is more or less how I paint the guns on my Dark Angels, oddly enough), building up the color slowly and carefully. A little edge highlight of Cold Grey on the blacks, and we're done. That's it. Five paints, two washes, and just look at it. Get a load of this guy. He rules.

What I like about this approach is that it can also - and will be on the next one - be used on other Zakus to provide a cohesive but interesting scheme. The triad of a dark, medium, and bright paint, where one part of the model is the dark highlighted with the medium and the other is the medium highlighted by the bright, seemed to work out well and didn't require a lot of paints or thought. If you replace the various reds with blues, that's basically Ramba Ral's custom colors, and if you use greens, that's the mass-production Zaku sorted. Once you get into Black Tri-Stars or Anavel Gato type designs, you're on your own, but this will get you most of the way there.

Rockfish

Char's Zaku II. Credit: Rockfish

I've never painted or done anything at all Gundam-related model-wise before this, and while I'll be the first to admit this is quite the unconventional entrance to that particular niche of the hobby, it has been a fun little thing to play with.

As you can tell from the limited colour palette in the above recipe, things will be moving fast on this scheme. You could probably knock out all the base coats in fifteen minutes or less if you wanted, and not that much more for any of the rest.

We start with a very aggressive zenithal of Tuskgor Fur over Vallejo German Panzer Grey primer through an airbrush, but I will mention that you could do this with a similar selection of rattle can primers or simply base coat the whole model in the main colour. The remaining base coats are uh, variable in that the Corvus Black will take no time to throw down, but the rich red is slightly more awkward. I chose to create it by mixing Corvus Black into Khorne Red until I had a tone I liked. It took surprisingly little of the black to get there, so move slowly.

As usual, I chose to make use of a wash to help define the recesses a bit; for that, I went to a very heavily thinned-down Null Oil and simply slopped it over the whole model. There are places where you can get away without this wash since the main zenithal is so stark, and we are working with dark colours for the rest, but I still like to get the additional free definition in the areas we aren't going to highlight. Normally, I avoid a simple black tone like Nuln, but in this case, since anything Gundam tends to lean towards clean cartoon colour tones, the 'simple' colour tone of this wash works fairly well.

Note that it's pretty important I went with a very heavily thinned wash, as while Nuln Oil out of the bottle would probably still get most of the effect you'd want, it would also leave a lot of staining, which is very hard to fix on a zenithal base coat. You could, of course, go back to Gundam techniques by relying on pin washes, but I tend to avoid those where I can these days.  It is an exceptionally slow technique, and in schemes where the plan is to do soft area highlights anyway, then the most visible pooling will be covered up by happenstance.

Speaking of highlights, we can smash those out fairly quickly on a model this small that also lacks significant convolution. For those, we come back to our base coat paint colours and add in very tiny specks of Screaming Skull incrementally to create our various highlight coats. Since this is a pretty light colour we're talking about, use as little as you can possibly fit on the brush while mixing it in, and even then, you might find it to be too much, requiring a dab of the original base colour to tone it down.

I did around 3-4 coats of successively brighter highlights in the areas I wanted to work on. It's worth mentioning that on a small model like this, it's pretty important to control both the paint's consistency and the direction from which you apply it. While I don't thin it as much as a glaze, only to the point before the paint 'breaks' and flows more like paste than water, this means we have to treat it pretty similarly to how one might when working on a glaze. This means that we pull the paint towards the brightest point during a brush stroke, so place the brush at the darkest end, where it will start from and move towards the brightest. The reason for this is to control where the bead gets left behind when you lift the brush. By which I mean, with thin paint and all paints in general, but it's less noticeable with viscous ones, the point where you lift the brush away from the model will have just a bit more paint left there, which can significantly affect the look of your transitions. This can be avoided by being mindful about leaving this extra blob somewhere it can get covered or is otherwise invisible, for example, dropping it off at the brightest point means that it shouldn't be noticeable if a section is slightly more opaque or brighter.

I generally lean towards these thin-layered highlights over glazes for the sake of speed. If I can get a good enough blend in 3-4 coats rather than 10+, I'll save that time whenever I have the choice on such a tiny model. Quick tip about transitions, glazed or otherwise: a varnish coat can save even a surprisingly rough blend, since a lot of the most noticeable differences are caused by the variance in finish caused by the paint being thinned so significantly!

Nearly there! Just the lenses and base now, starting with the first, I did a very simple gem effect with just Caliban Green and Screaming Skull. Since these are small gems that aren't particularly the focus of the design, besides the mono-eye aspect, I suppose I found something simple more than good enough.

The base is actually my normal BattleTech scheme! Start with a thin layer of Vallejo Grey Sand, paint it Steel Legion Drab, and then wash it in Agrax Earthshade. That's it to the tone, I really don't feel like it needs a drybrush or really any extra work on something intended to be small scale, besides some tufts and bushes after a matte varnish coat, of course. For the plant life, I made use of a combination of Woodland Scenics Bushes, torn up a bit for the larger shrubs and then Gamers Grass Tiny Tufts in a Dry and Light Green colour tone for the grasses around the shrubs. (Remember to cluster plants! It looks far more natural to have bunched up growth rather than to randomly scatter little bits.)

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website and more.

Delta Reign - November 6

The best SIRs are for Rayquaza and Raikou, and there are Illustration Rares for the big green dragon's weather trio mates  Groudon and Kyogre as well.

Pokemon sets FAQ

The list above tells you every set released in Pokémon TCG history - but there's more to the story of Pokémon cards than that! Read on for answers to some of the most common questions about sets, to help you get a handle on the hobby.

How many Pokémon sets are there?

As of January 2026, there have been 127 English language Pokémon sets that were legal to use in organized play at the time they were printed.

The pace of Pokémon sets picked up last year, with a huge bubble of fan hype and interest for releases around January 2025's Prismatic Evolutions, and shows no sign of abating. In fact, this year (2026) is the 30th anniversary of Pokémon TCG's original launch, so there's every chance the hype train could speed up over the coming months!

If you want to store a large collection of cards, our guide to Pokémon card sizes has their dimensions and weight so you can work out exactly how much space you'll need.

How many Pokémon sets are released every year?

Around three to four Regular Pokémon sets are released each year - usually accompanied by two to four special sets and smaller promotional packs.

For example, in 2025 there were seven sets in total, including:

  • Four regular sets - Journey Together, Destined Rivals, Mega Evolution, and Phantasmal Flames.
  • Three special sets - Prismatic Evolutions, White Flare and Black Bolt.

What are the different types of Pokémon sets?

There are three main types of Pokémon TCG sets:

  1. Regular sets: The TCG's mainline releases, Regular sets are the 'tentpole' events of each season, releasing at roughly regular intervals each year with a large number of cards. Regular sets are normally available in quite a few different product types, including booster boxes of 36 ten-card booster packs.
  2. Special sets: Also sometimes called 'Special Collections', these sets generally have a smaller overall card list and a specific theme that underpins their most prominent cards. Special sets don't get booster boxes and are normally sold in Elite Trainer Boxes (ETBs) and small promotional packs like Binder Collections.
  3. Mini-sets: A catch-all term for all smaller set releases that don't merit the 'Special Collection' label, but are still a distinct collection of new or reprinted cards. These usually come in their own seasonal or promotional packs, like the three-card Trick or Trade mini packs released around Halloween, or promo tins.

Which Pokémon sets are worth money?

Generally, the older and more scarce a Pokémon set is, the more valuable it is. First-edition copies of Base Set, the original Pokémon set, are worth the most money. Individual booster packs can sell for thousands of dollars, and booster boxes are even more ludicrously priced. Many of the individual cards from this set can be just as valuable (if not moreso), provided they're still in good condition.

While this is the ultimate chase set for hardcore collectors, most sets from the early 2000s are hard to find in the form of a sealed booster box.

On the other hand, modern Pokémon cards while never reaching the heights of the older sets, can still be worth a pretty penny. Right now the Pokémon card market is booming, with many recent cards selling for hundreds of dollars.

What's the best Pokémon set?

The best Pokémon TCG set is the one that has your favorite cards in it - which could be any of them! Sorry we can't be more precise, but there's really no 'best Pokémon set' that applies to everyone.

If you're chasing the most expensive cards, you might consider the oldest sets (as described above) the best, as they give you a chance at pulling something worth new car money.

If you're in love with a particular chase card that's desirable right now, then that card's set might be the best for you - Bubble Mew lovers will likely rank Paldean Fates highly, while Moonbreon stans probably rate Evolving Skies.

If you want to buy the best Pokémon set for you, decide which cards or card types bring you most joy - and why - then find the sets that include those cards. If you're getting into Pokémon card collecting to fill a binder with your favorites, make a hit list and go hunting! If you're building an all-star team of super-strong cards, our guide to most powerful Pokémon in the game can help you in the quest.

And - for now - that's it for our guide to Pokémon TCG sets! If you've got a favorite to support, or just want to join the hype about upcoming sets, come hop into the Pokémon TCG discussion in our Discord community! Chances are we're also salivating over the latest chase SIR, too.

Alternatively, we've got lots more Pokémon TCG guides to help you along - we can even help you answer the twin age-old questions - how many Pokémon are there, and how many Pokémon cards are there?

title: CRAB RAGE! review - a board game more exciting to say than play
content:
Our Verdict

CRAB RAGE!, for its all-caps title, isn't much to shout about. It tries to toe the line between precise strategy game and rollercoaster thematic title, but it excels as neither. The rules are fiddly and lack impact, and despite a few clever design choices, don't always make sense thematically. Things run smoother after a few plays, but there's not much reward for repeating the experience. The results are fun, but notably flawed.

Pros
  • Visually wonderful
  • Unique theme
  • Some clever mechanics
Cons
  • Limited replay value
  • Several design flaws
  • Hit-and-miss theme

I want to love CRAB RAGE!. A board game this wacky is usually right up my alley. Sadly, though, reality has come crashing down, like a buff crab doing a sick elbow drop.

CRAB RAGE! is vibrant and unique. Once you clear the surprisingly chunky rulebook, you're in for a snappy, smooth ride. And I certainly can't accuse CRAB RAGE! of being boring. This is an area majority game that makes many interesting, thematic decisions.

Unfortunately, I think CRAB RAGE! is more complex than it needs to be. For every clever mechanic, there's one that gums the wheels. 'Inelegant' is the word that comes to mind. At times, CRAB RAGE! has all the elegance of a botched pile driver.

If you couldn't tell, this is a game of macho wrestling madness. Each of you manages a vibrant team of Crab wrestlers, who are vying for glory across several battlegrounds. If you have the most fans in an area at the end of play, you earn Glory. The player with the most Glory wins. How do you earn fans, you ask? PUNCHING EACH OTHER IN THE FACE.

That's not all there is to it, though. Just like real-life pro wrestling, spectacle matters. It's not enough to have the most Muscle. There must be dynamic team-ups, dramatic betrayals, and last-minute twists.

Your team of wrestlers is represented by dice, with each die's current value representing their physical prowess. The team with the highest total Muscle in an arena at round-end gets to add fan tokens. The more crabs that were battling for that bucket, the more fans you attract.

Each turn, you'll perform one action from a growing tableau. Actions require you to spend varying amounts of Rage, red cubes that represent your hot-blooded athlete's mounting adrenaline.

Actions start out simple. You can move a crab from place to place, triggering an on-entry ability on the arena's billboard. Or, you might decide to 'Go Clam', changing your die value to five then charging into a new zone. You might stay put and Smash an opponent, reducing their die's value equal to the Rage spent. Or you could split up an established a team.

That one takes some more explaining. When a crab moves to a new arena, its manager decides whether it teams up with another team's crabs. Doing so ups your Muscle, but it halves the fans you might acquire at round-end. Alternatively, you can go solo, which creates more opponents for that arena, but yields higher rewards. I'm a big fan of this mechanic, which replicates the ludicrous team-ups of WWE and its ilk.

From the second round onward, new dramatic flourishes become available. You can shunt crabs into other zones based on their Muscle value, switch Muscle or position with a rival, boost your own Muscle, or simply spam fans in your current space.

CRAB RAGE! presents a vast web of decisions. Will you blow all your Rage on powerful actions in one round, knowing you'll take fewer actions in the next? Will you accept a tactical loss in one arena to gain Rage instead of fans? Will you spread out to gather end-of-round billboard bonuses, or is it better to hunker down and hoard fans in one spot?

There are so many options, they actually have less impact. With the right action tableau, tactical advantages are easily reversed on the next player's turn. That on its own isn't an issue. Rubber-banding is a thrilling part of many games, particularly those that lean more thematic than strategic.

CRAB RAGE!, however, can't quite decide what it wants to be. It tries to offer precise, tactical gameplay with its many decision points, but their low impact leaves you more frustrated than fulfilled. Plus, the power level of different choices vary drastically.

A prime example is the Special Move. Each crab team has a unique once-per-game ability, a fancy flourish that can turn the tide of battle. They're all pretty good, but one among them is clearly superior. The Jurassic Thorax team's special power is Ramprage, which builds two Rage for each of their crabs in a single arena. Because Rage fuels actions, that gives you two or three extra actions in a round, if you time things right. Use this towards game-end, when nobody else has Rage to spend, and you've got a serious runaway advantage.

The power isn't broken enough to guarantee a win, but Jurassic Thorax has a better chance than most. It's the kind of imbalance that can be laughed off in a thematic board game, but crunch-lovers might find it unfair.

All this leaves a tactical player feeling deflated. Unfortunately, thematic players won't be too thrilled either. CRAB RAGE! simply isn't consistent with its ludonarrative.

For me, the biggest sinner is the Hardcore fans mechanic. You'll collect Hardcore fans through end-of-round billboard bonuses, and they're used for a bidding mini-game at game-end. Before you total everyone's fans in an arena, managers have a chance to bid Hardcore fans, adding them to your team's total as a last-minute substitution. It could swing you the win, but you've no idea how much your buddies are bidding, so it's a gamble.

What does this have to do with wrestling? What aspect of building a career in the ring does this represent? It feels illogical, and it adds very little to the experience.

There are more of these minor rules that add more complexity, but not much else. Style bonuses give you extra fans if you're the first person to take an action. There's a dice-rolling mini-game to decide tie-breaks. There's another mechanic to decide ties at the end. Dice 'mutate' with a re-roll if you hoard too much Rage. Billboards have on-entry effects on dice moving to an arena, and they must be rotated between locations every round.

CRAB RAGE! isn't a difficult game. It is, thanks to these little rules, far fiddlier than it needs to be. Too much time is lost flipping through the rulebook. It's those moments most of all where hype dies down. The crowd goes from shouts to murmurs. They start to think about a snack break. Too many of these intervals, and you might lose their attention completely.

That clunkiness can be solved by experience, but you need to want a second showing. CRAB RAGE!, for all its intricacies, feels much the same from game to game. A tournament score log in the back of the rulebook encourages you to undertake an epic Royal Rumble of repeat plays, but it's not varied enough to justify this.

I like CRAB RAGE! well enough. But I wanted to love it. It's neither heel nor hero in my eyes - just another jobber who's not flashy enough for a headline match.

title: Trench Crusade October Rules Review: The Tabletop Battles Hot Take
content:
Welcome, all, to the latest Trench Crusade article at Tabletop Battles, where we’re taking a look at the game's latest rules release. This rules update focuses on the Court of the Seven-Headed Serpent, with a full faction rework, including all seven Sins, plus unit changes. So grab your sulfur tea and your brimstone biscuits, and sit back and come with us on this journey into Hell itself. 

Credit: darius_minis

What’s Changed in the Court of the Seven Headed Serpent? 

Well, pretty much everything! This is a full faction overhaul. We’re talking Faction rules and how Sin Markers work, additions and changes to the Armory, updates to the Sins, with variance to how Sin Markers are generated, and some Unit changes.

Faction Rules

The biggest and most immediate change here is the way in which your Goetic Powers are fuelled. No longer do you power your spells from Blood Markers taken from non-Demon models, but now when you cause a Blood Marker to an enemy, you may instead give the attacking model a Sin Marker, up to a max of 6. These are then used to power your Spells. You can gain Sin Markers through other means, like abilities or Battlekit, so there’s no fear that you are losing out on damage output. Counter to this, enemy models may remove a Sin Marker instead of placing a Blood Marker on one of your models. 

Goetic Powers, Abilities, and Spells are largely the same, swapping out the use of Blood Markers for Sin Markers. So Spells can be powered through Sin Markers, and can be taken from any friendly unit that has a Sin Marker on them. 

Along with all of that is the inclusion of new Goetic Powers that any Warband may take. There are some Powers that have stayed, like Slavemaster and Blessing of the Serpent Moon, but new ones like Infernal Challenge, which adds a simple +1 Injury Dice if the target model has the Tough Keywords, can add some new spice to the mix. 

Sin Changes

If a complete Faction Rule overhaul wasn’t enough, then what about each and every Sin getting a well-deserved glow-up? That’s right! In this update, each Sin gets their own special rules, Battlekit, Goetic Powers, as well as changes to list building. Now some units may not be taken with certain Sins. Here’s a brief look at each of the Sins: 

  • Pride: Pride is your strength. Defiance is your purpose. Wield the Morningstar’s Light and armaments to bring your enemy to their knees. Use Open Terrain and elevation to your advantage, all the while ensuring the safety of your Demonic units as your Wretched throw themselves in front of incoming enemy attacks. 
  • Greed: War has a price. A price that Mammom is all too happy to pay, for far greater riches can be gained. Sin Markers are gained by targeting certain priced units that decrease in threshold each Turn, and your Spells and Battlekit only work when affecting targets with a certain (Ducat) worth. 
  • Lust: Turn the Sin of the Flesh to your advantage, as your mortal Non-Demonic Units can be used to extract more Sin Markers. Battlekit and Powers ask you and your opponent how much they are willing to gamble to achieve their goals or avoid pain. 
  • Envy: Hell Knights envy those above them, and as such, Sorcerers and Praetors may not be taken in this warband. Instead, you may take at least 2 and up to 5 Hell Knights, gaining a unique Glorious Deed to use each game, as well as free Sin Markers to one of your Knights. Sin Markers are also generated for nearby allies by taking enemies out of Action or Downing them. Take the weapons of your enemy as your own, for why should you not covet such power? 
  • Gluttony: Indulge on your enemies as you wear them down with Melee attacks, culminating in a feast for your allies. Your Elites are harder to hit, and your hungry Troops are nimbler, as they look for their next meal. Your Powers and Battlekit aim to keep you alive and hungry for more. 
  • Wrath: Use the very fires of Hell to lay your enemies low, as attacks with the Fire Keyword grant Sin Markers. Powers and Battlekit play around with the Fire Keyword, allowing models to add it to all their Melee Attacks, or even turn the very ground itself to fire. 
  • Sloth: Ensure inevitable victory by converting Success rolls to Risky Success Rolls for yourself, and slowing down the tempo of your opponent. Your Spells and Battlekit punish enemy models that have already activated, as well as pulling them out of position. 

Unit Changes

  • Praetor: Still the unholy killing machine we all know and love/fear, but now as an added bonus they generate a Sin Marker for free whenever they activate! Useful for keeping things running smoothly. 
  • Sorcerer: Blessing of the Serpent Moon is now purchasable instead of an innate upgrade, and they come with everyone’s favorite Inferno spell built in. You can also buy the LEADER keyword for 5 Ducats.
  • Hellknight: You may purchase the FEAR keyword for 5 Ducats. No other changes needed for perfection it seems. 
  • Hunter of the Left-Hand Path: A subtle change you might miss, no more shields! A big change everyone will notice, the Left Hand Path ability itself now has a hard distance limit of 24 inches. This will make turn one Alpha Strikes more difficult to pull off but not impossible, as well as making it less of an ever oppressive board presence.
  • Wretched: The classic bloodbags now get a bonus to dashing if a Yoke Fiend is within line of sight and 8 inches of them.
  • Pit Locust: Cricket/Locust noises, no change here
  • Yoke Fiend: No more Hateful, so they no longer mandate charging Mortals within 12 inches. And they gain a power up! If you manage to get 3 Sin Markers on your various fiends, they all get +1 Dice to Melee attacks.
  • Desecrated Saint: From a simple giant smashing machine to a powerful centerpiece, it’s got two new auras! One gives all friendly demons that activate within 1 inch of it a Sin Marker. The second makes all enemy models within 6 inches of it not count as Friendly for their own faction. It also gained a few keywords for the pile, IGNORE CUMBERSOME and IGNORE DIFFICULT TERRAIN seem to be the most impactful. It also no longer gets slowed down from standing after being downed, so the Saint is going to be an issue as long as it is alive. 

Note, these changes are for the warband not devoted to any single Sin. Each Head of the Serpent comes with their own changes to various models that may be gone over in more detail in a future article.

Credit: Darius_minis

Final Thoughts

DGMP: This is an insane glow up. Going from the faction with the least variety in viable playstyles to what is no doubt now the most will rejuvenate the Court immensely. It is really hard to sum up all of this, really. It is practically 7 different armies in a trenchcoat saying it is a single faction. Frankly this is the upgrade that the Court needed, giving it a level of flavor and style that it was sorely lacking before the Sins all got the attention that they so desperately needed. I was a Pride main before this update and with all of the shiny new toys available I am unsure if I can remain such a purist in the future! Honestly I have nothing but good things to say and glowing praise to give regarding this update. If this is the new standard level of quality we can expect from Trench Crusade going forward, next year is going to be absolutely insane.

Zaros: There is so much to explore within this update that you are going to be lost in the list building mines for a while. Faction wide battlekit additions enable new strategies and variant specific battlekit help hone playstyles within the various sins. Every choice feels impactful and worth the choice now in comparison to the pool of similarity that court used to swim in. I can’t wait to see the insanity people are going to come up with and the wild lists (I’m looking at you double saint and you as well triple sin eater) that are going to be on the table! This is the time court players have been waiting for since the April rules review, eat up and enjoy the hellish buffet that has been presented!

Dandy: I’m still getting over the shock of how big these changes are. The others have hinted at the innumerable ways you can play this army now, but I’m glad we can finally see more Yoke Fiends and Wretched out on the board more consistently. With a plethora of new Spells, Abilities, and Battlekits, there’s a lot to try, and it’ll bring a refreshing experience not only for Court players, but for everyone. Factory Fortress Inc. has done a great job with this update, and along with the Carcass Front rules, we're seeing what they're capable of post 1.0 release, and I have to say, things are looking good. Very good. Sorry faithful, it's time to build up some Demons... Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. title: The Halo wargame finally reveals an army of Covenant miniatures, and they're sick
content:
On Friday, UK based miniature maker Mantic Games revealed a complete range of Covenant miniatures for its Halo miniature game Halo: Flashpoint. We're talking San'Shyuum Prophets, Sangheili Honour Guard, Mgalekgolo Hunters, even the High Prophet of Regret: if Master Chief filled it full of bullets during the Human-Covenant war, it's probably getting a model.

The Covenant forces will debut in a new big-box faction pack expansion, Halo: Flashpoint Judgement. You'll need a copy of the Halo: Flashpoint base game (or a friend with one) to play, but it's a pretty bumper box set.

Judgement contains the following brand new miniatures:

  • The Prophet of Regret
  • A lower ranking San'Shyuum Prophet
  • Two Sangheili Elite Honour Guard
  • A Sangheili Elite Major
  • Two Sangheili Elite Rangers with jet packs
  • Two Mgalekgolo Hunters
  • A new Kig-Yar Jackal Sniper with a Beam rifle
  • A new Kig-Yar Jackal Freebooter with a plasma pistol and energy shield
1/7

It also comes with eight models that were released previously as Banished forces: three Unggoy Grunts (two of them assault troops, one a conscript); a Kig-Yar Jackal freebooter with a needler and an energy shield; and a team of four Sangheili Elite Mercenaries with a variety of weapons.

Judgment comes with all the tokens, cards, and lurid pink faction dice needed to field the Covenant in a game. It also has a game mat, and enough cardboard terrain for you to combine its battlefield with one from the starter set and play a double-sized 'Big Battle'.

I've recently received a review sample of the revised Spartan starter set for Halo: Flashpoint, and I can speak to the component quality for the line: the models are very detailed and need no assembly, and the cardboard terrain is sturdy and easy to construct.

When Flashpoint launched, it was effectively a tabletop version of Halo: Infinite multiplayer, with players typically fielding teams of four Spartans (though there four Elites were available at launch). The range has since been expanded substantially with two big faction box sets: The Rise of the Banished, which introduced models for the Jiralhanae Brutes; and Feet First Into Hell, which added the luckless humans of the UNSC. Add-on packs have added more troops like Jackals and Grunts.

It's still a very low model count game, typically four Spartan-equivalent miniatures per side, but there are optional rules for playing with double-sized forces across two game boards, and using points-based list construction to tinker with your team line-up. Judgment contains more than enough miniatures to give you a lot of list-building options in this format.

1/5

Judgment isn't the only new Halo product in Mantic's lineup. The firm has also revealed more details about Halo: Campaign Evolved - The board game. Designed for head to head play, or for one player to play against the AI, this narrative campaign game follows Master Chief's iconic first foray against the Covenant. The set contains a new miniature for John 117 and another for a Sangheili Zealot, plus standees to represent the other Covenant forces the Chief mows through. Both of the plastic minis come with rules cards so you can use them in Flashpoint.

There are two other small but entertaining products on their way as well. First there's a miniature for Sergeant Johnson, everyone's favorite cigar-chomping UNSC officer. And there's also a score tracker designed to look like Master Chief's second AI companion, Joyeuse.

1/2

All these new releases are available for pre-order on the Mantic Games webstore. The studio expects to ship them this December, so hopefully in time for Christmas.

I was very impressed with Halo: Flashpoint when I tested the launch version - it didn't get a scored review at the time, but you can find a lot of my thoughts in this article. It's in contention for a place in our guide to the best miniature wargames when I give that it's much-needed overhaul.

With the Covenant now confirmed, what other models do you want to see make the leap from the Halo videogames and onto the tabletop? Come and join the free Wargamer Discord community if you've got thoughts!

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Voice of Command, by Richard Swan
content:
Image credit: Games Workshop

If it wasn't for Australian Rules Football, it's entirely possible that I would never have gotten into Warhammer.

Believe it or not, Louisville was the modern birthplace of the sport in the US with the first match against a team from Cincinnati taking place in 1996. That was a decade in the rearview when I was playing for the Louisville Kings, of course, but one day I got to chatting with a teammate about our shared interest in science fiction and he gushed about Warhammer 40,000. Seeing he'd caught my interest, the very next practice he brought a few of his omnibuses for me to borrow- and that's how I learned about Eisenhorn, Gaunt's Ghosts, and Ciaphas Cain.

One of my enduring memories of that time saw me sitting on the steps of the family Summer cottage on Cape Cod next to my future wife Jimi, hunched over that loaner copy of Eisenhorn until it grew too dark outside to read. Dan Abnetts' depiction of the world of the Chaos-tainted Saruthi in Xenos, with its strange coloration and unnatural angles, spoke to a familiar kind of eldritch horror that had me turning page after page to see what would come next.

Similarly, Abnett's descriptions of plummeting temperatures and appearance of ice during warp manifestations echoed back to my lifelong love of ghost stories, and to this day remains some of the most evocative and unsettling depictions of Chaos in the Black Library.

I was, as they say, hooked.

Now in the present, having read many more books in the Black Library, I find this "horror-story sensibility" of Chaos to be the exception rather than the norm. Oh, we get plenty of descriptions of strange mutations and plague zombies, pink and blue unearthly horrors and uncomfortably alluring beings with lobster claw hands, but I always sit up and take notice when a writer brings something new and distinctive to the table when it comes to describing Chaos. Something that recaptures that early sense of discomfited wonder at the unspeakable malignancy of the warp and its Ruinous Powers.

And with his Black Library novel debut, Voice of Command, author Richard Swan did precisely that.

When Voice of Command was revealed on the mothership, the response in the community was somewhat muted. I mean, c'mon, the deck is probably stacked against any book not named Pandaemonium that's teased alongside a new offering from Peter Fehervari, right? But the rather uninspiring cover art (illustrated by Alex Gor, whose last name makes drawing for Warhammer almost seem predestined) alongside a rather generic title and a general sense of 'Cadian fatigue' wasn't winning Swan any nods for Most Anticipated Novel of 2026.

But as it turns out, Voice of Command is one of the year's more interesting surprises.

The Story

Voice of Command puts us alongside the Cadian 2002nd Mechanized Regiment on the shrine world of Nymea. They're two years into a grueling campaign to push back a traitorous Ecclesiarchy and Guard that have succumbed to the taint of corruption. A malefic blue star sometimes appears in the night sky, its toxic light uncomfortable to look at and heralding misfortune. The Imperial vox is taken over each night with broadcasts of unlistenable heresy, and strange crystals have begun to sprout from the earth.

On the eve of their push to retake the capital city of Saint Stanislava's Adoration, the Cadians must not only navigate the schemes of the enemy, but tensions between Cadians and Nymeans, Inquisitorial meddling, creeping corruption in the ranks, and the misfortunes of war.

The action focuses on Colonel "Venom" Velterson- whose nickname is almost an afterthought, adroitly avoiding coming off as cheesy- and a number of the officers and troopers of the Cadian regiment. Swan plays with a relatively large cast here, helpfully including a nicely detailed Dramatis Personae so you don't need to backtrack if someone slips your mind. The POV frequently shifts, but always in focused service to the greater narrative flow (think Robert Rath's excellent Fall of Cadia here).

As the Cadian troops slog it out in the streets and alleys of the city, an airborne Kasrkin unit attempts insertion for a decapitation strike. All the while, a monstrous- and monstrously familiar- threat from within threatens to destroy the Cadians before they can reclaim the city.

Image credit: Games Workshop

The Crystal Method

I was blown away by Swan's ability to generate genuine dread and suspense almost from the jump. It helps that the story's protagonists are Imperial Guard, and in being "regular" humans they're in many ways the most relatable of all Warhammer 40K's factions. That makes them a perfect foil for the cosmic and body horror elements that increase in volume as the story races along. When someone goes to move a corpse only to find it crunches like broken glass, you tend to sit up and take notice.

As a work of military science fiction, this had the same clarity of writing and terrific pacing that made Abnett's Gaunt's Ghosts stories so riveting. There's little slowdown to the story; once things kick off (and they do almost immediately), the rest of the book is essentially one scene as the battle grinds towards its inexorable conclusion. This may be Swan's debut Black Library novel, but hardly his first. He's penned two fantasy trilogies (Empire of the Wolf, and the ongoing Great Silence trilogy), as well as a science-fiction one (the Art of War trilogy), and is a Sunday Times bestselling author.

That deep experience was clearly evident in Voice of Command, not only in the narrative elements he brought with him, but the ones he declined to use. One of the most refreshing parts of this story is that while the main characters are Cadians, that's only modestly relevant to the story beyond just providing a source of friction between them and the native Nymean regiment. If you give this one a miss due to that aforementioned Cadian fatigue, it's worth having a rethink.

Finally, the writing is also terrifically descriptive without bogging down the pace. Here's one example, a moment of battlefield fatigue that's almost poetic in its expression:

"Was this it? Could this truly be it forever? Did they just move from one battlefield to the next, fighting and dying? Uncountable staging areas? Bivouacs, tents, trenches - trench foot - lung rot, brain rot, dysentery, venereal disease? The false, desperate love of a camp follower, the illicit drag on a narcotic cigarette, shots of life-shortening spirits distilled in an ammunition can? Was it nothing but mud and blood, the sight of yet another trooper being cut in half by artillery, listening to the resigned sighs of the old guard, the disbelieving weeping of the fresh recruits? Was it sitting in the cramped holds of mass troop conveyances in the cold depths of space, the mind-altering - mind-ending, life-ending - horrors of the warp? Was it just battle after battle, round after round, bullets and lasgun beams and chainsword swipes, until her life was ended by the enemy, or her own hand - or worse, by completely random bad luck? Would she one day be killed in a vehicle collision or a Geller field failure? Would they be subjected to the capricious whims of the Inquisition, or the bottomless incompetence of the Administratum? Would she be carpet-bombed by her own side, stand on a land mine, get shot by a sniper?

Just one more mile - one more planet, one more system, one more campaign, one more sector. But it never ended. That was the truth of it. It was infinity, and the worst sort, too. In the grim darkness of her future, of all their futures, there was only war.

Sublime.

Image credit: Games Workshop

Final Thoughts

Of all the criteria I use to assess a book, one of the simplest and most informal is, how long did it take me to read it? Did I grind through the book, reading only during my usual pre-bedtime ritual? Did I carry the book around me, happy to squeeze in a few pages at every opportunity? Something in the middle? It's been a minute since I tore through a book as quickly as I did this one.

Overall, Voice of Command is a cracking read and a real statement of what Swan is able to do in the Black Library if given the opportunity. I feel a bit foolish for having done so, but I did indeed judge a book by its cover- though in fairness, a look at the book's product page on the webstore shows that the marketing team's own copy was itself a bit lackluster (a "heart-rending Warhammer 40,000 novel," really?)

But that aside, Swan blends a veteran writer's skill and craft with a fresh take on the horrors of Chaos, and nestling all that within an Astra Militarum novel gave it a lot of room to breathe. This is certainly one of the year's standout books, and I recommend it without hesitation.

title: Dedicated Warhammer 40k player tracks every one of his minis' stats and stories over 250 games
content:
Few Warhammer 40k players can claim to know their armies as well as Calvin Foster, an Adeptus Custodes player from Des Moines, Iowa. Since April 2022 he's recorded detailed stats for his army in over 250 games - not just the wins and losses, not just which units score points and which are destroyed, but in so much granular detail that he knows exactly what each of his Custodians has achieved in service to the Emperor.

Foster started playing Warhammer 40k, and the Custodes, in spring 2021. "I thought it would be cool if each model had a name, leaning into the 'Earning of a Name' aspect of Custodes lore", he recalls. With the help of a buddy who owned a 3D printer he began making nameplates. Then, he says, "I had the epiphany that if they all had unique names, I could track what each model accomplished in a game".

Foster began tracking data in April 2022, just after a dataslate update to the Custodes' 9th edition rules. His record keeping is exhaustive. He brings a "printed out Excel sheet with five pages, one for each round, and the name of every model I'm using that game" to every battle.

Each round, he records how much damage a model does; how many and what type of models they killed; actions completed; objective markers held; assists; if a model dies; and special notes if they do something extraordinarily good or bad. In cases where it's not clear who did what, like a squad collectively dismantling a Repulsor Executioner, he randomizes who gets the glory.

"Once the game is over, I'll note how many list building points the models they killed are worth, and how many victory points they earned… and enter it into my spreadsheet where I track each model's stats over their whole career". This lets Foster "track things like win rate, KDR, and VP earned per game". He aggregates data from individual models to generate the expected performance of typical units.

He's also fulfilling his original plan of granting his Custodians deed names. "When someone does something extraordinary they 'Earn a Name', be it a good one or bad one, related to the feat performed or failed", he explains. As it stands, Foster says "my original Trajan model has the most good names earned, at five, and one of my grav tanks, Masada, has the most fail names earned, also at five".

Foster has been able to track trends in unit performance across editions. In 10th edition, Caladius Grav Tanks were "our best and most reliable datasheet all edition, and haven't been nerfed or buffed once since the edition started", whereas "Trajan fell off when our 10th edition codex dropped".

I actually spoke to Foster quite early this year, before the new edition launched, so I checked in with him recently to find out about his hopes for the Custodes' upcoming Warhammer 40k 11th edition codex release. "I'm digging the increase in durability, and I like how the army rule has some flexibility to it and requires more thought than just smashing the lethals or sustained button like a caveman", he says.

Foster says his data doesn't have a huge impact on his list building decisions "other than [identifying] 'this unit is good, let's take three of them'". When there's a choice between models in his collection that could fulfil a role, he takes "whichever models of that datasheet have the fewest games logged yet".

But he does admit to developing superstitions. "One of the Grav Tanks, Mammoth, has underperformed the other two in the kills category, but has wildly outperformed them and everything else in my army in the VP earned category". He says that's quite common in the data: "each datasheet seems to have one or two models that perform much higher or lower than its brethren".

Foster says he makes game decisions "based on what will help me when, versus what will help a model's stats", and ""I always root for the underperformers, but in no way do I put my thumb on the scale". "Letting things happen as they may also adds to the narrative of the whole thing, instead of trying to 'fix' things", he adds.

When you put the same models on the table again and again it's   inevitable that you'll develop stories for them, but Foster really has taken it to the next level. Tracking unit stats is a good tool for competitive players, but Foster shows how well it works as a prompt for developing the narrative of your army. Do you have any minis that you've developed a real story around? The community in the Wargamer Discord would love to see pics and hear their saga.
